_comment: The presentation layer over the fleet register (https://loki.orangecat.ch/api/fleet/map). The register says WHAT EXISTS and WHERE; this file says how bitbaum shows it. Keyed by canonical slug = repository name. A register row without a `what` here is not shown at all. `stage` is one of product | pilot | concept | next, chosen by what a visitor can verify — never by the register's kind: a `client-app` row is a PILOT (built for a real organisation, in real use, no commercial terms), never a client. `tags` are the FIELD facet on the home grid and must come from `tagOrder`. `story` is the venture's own page. `shot: false` keeps a placeholder page's screenshot off the site.

product.title: Product
product.lede: Running and public — in beta, yours to use today.

pilot.title: Pilot
pilot.lede: Built for a real organisation and in real use. No commercial terms — a working answer, offered first.

concept.title: Concept
concept.lede: Built to apply with, before anyone asked. Working demos on public or mock data.

next.title: Next
next.lede: Named, not built. Listed so the list is honest.

_adopterAliases: The package registry names adopters by REPOSITORY, which is not always the venture's slug (the Hirnli app lives in bitbaum/hirnli while the register row is revamp-info). Map repo -> slug here so 'what uses this package' can link. An adopter with no venture page renders as plain text — which is honest: it is a real adopter the site does not show.

orangecat.name: OrangeCat
orangecat.pillarRole: How value reaches people. Any identity — a person, a pseudonym, an AI agent — takes part in the economy without a bank's permission, and Bitcoin settles it.
orangecat.story: OrangeCat sets up ways to earn, Bitcoin settles, and you stay in charge. Any identity — a person, a pseudonym, an AI agent — takes part in the economy without asking a bank or a platform first. Pay-links work today; funding, lending and the Cat's allocation are governed in Solon and built in the open.

loki.name: Loki
loki.pillarRole: How work gets done. Dispatch it to a fleet of AI agents and people, watch it, approve it, ship it — agents execute where the code lives.
loki.story: Loki is the operating system for people running real AI agents: dispatch work to a fleet, watch it, approve it, ship it. Agents execute where the code lives; you command from anywhere. It builds and deploys every product on this page, including itself.

solon.name: Solon
solon.pillarRole: How decisions get made together. Bitcoin-signed votes and versioned policies, so nobody has to trust the count — including the rule that pays originators.
solon.story: Proposals, Bitcoin-signed votes, versioned policies and an append-only audit trail. Nobody has to trust Solon's count: every decision is a signed record anyone can re-tally. It governs OrangeCat's spending ceiling and the rule that routes a share of revenue back to whoever originated the code.

revamp-info.name: Hirnli
revamp-info.story: Finds the right Swiss foundations for a non-profit, drafts the application, and keeps the relationship history. In daily use at Revamp-IT, the Zürich non-profit it was built inside.

evig.name: evig
evig.what: Access to intelligence, affordable for everyone
evig.story: Refurbished hardware, repair, and courses from Revamp-IT, a Zürich digital-inclusion non-profit. The site, the shop and the workshop calendar.

datacat.name: DataCat
datacat.story: Capture data through a form, a product scan or a bulk import, and get structured records back. Built for teams that keep records but not databases.

petvity.name: Petvity
petvity.what: Your pet has a signal. Now you can read it.
petvity.story: One daily check-in builds a living record of a pet — what changed, when, and what a vet or sitter needs to know. A humane adoption network sits on the same records.

substrata.name: Substrata
substrata.what: What moved among the constraints on technological progress
substrata.story: A running log of the physical chokepoints — energy, materials, fabrication — as dated events, so that 'progress is limited by atoms' is a list you can read rather than a sentence.

surf-your-life.name: Surf Your Life
surf-your-life.what: Burnout and long COVID, treated at the biology
surf-your-life.story: A psychiatrist-led programme for burnout and long COVID that works from metabolic biology rather than symptom management. The programme site and its intake.

botsmann.name: Botsmann
botsmann.story: Considered counsel from AI specialists in law, health, research and more — private by construction. Validating whether people want this, before building more of it.

aoz-housing.name: AOZ Begleitung
aoz-housing.story: Shared-living management with a placement engine for refugee housing: compatibility matching across 38 factors, incidents, maintenance, and a resident portal for expenses, rules and votes. Running as a pilot on a real shared flat. AOZ is not a customer; the product exists to show what one would get.

kivvi.name: kivvi
kivvi.what: The operating system for the circular economy
kivvi.story: An ERP where every device keeps its history — donation, repair, refurbishment, resale. In production at Revamp-IT, run as a favour, not a contract.

vitareba.name: Vita
vitareba.what: A clinic, with its patients in the loop
vitareba.story: Patient portal and clinician console for a metabolic-psychiatry and longevity practice. One real clinic uses it; nobody pays for it yet.

s-ink.name: S.Ink
s-ink.story: The studio's own site: artists, work, booking. Built and hosted as a favour.

sbb-fundbuero.name: Nordbahn Fundbüro
sbb-fundbuero.what: Lost on the train, while you are still on it
sbb-fundbuero.story: Report a lost item bound to the real journey from Swiss open transport data, so staff can look while the train is still moving. Items reported within thirty minutes are mostly recovered; after a day, mostly not. A concept on mock data — not affiliated with SBB, built to show them.

reparaturbonus-zh.name: Reparaturbonus
reparaturbonus-zh.what: Repair instead of replace — the City of Zürich's bonus, as it should work
reparaturbonus-zh.story: Find a workshop, start the repair, claim the CHF 100. A concept for the City of Zürich's repair bonus, built to apply with.

heidi.name: Heidi
heidi.story: Understand what was said, then write back in it. Sign in, practise in a group, and Heidi answers in the conversation when you name her.

printcraft.name: PrintCraft
printcraft.story: Turn separate photos into one shared scene. A concept waiting for its first user.

camille-boulangerie.name: Camille
camille-boulangerie.story: A handover site for a bakery, produced by the OrangeCat site factory as a demonstration of what a small business gets in an afternoon.

causius.name: Causius
causius.what: Law, the same shape as Diplodoctor

extras.name: Annushka
extras.story: Works, events and a way to book a sitting for a painter from Ukraine in Zürich. Built and hosted as a favour.
extras._why: static site plus a dead :4030 api; does not fit an apps.conf row

packages_lede: The shared code every product is built from. Each one exists because a second app was about to write the same thing. Open a package to read why it exists, how it works, and where it sits in the studio.

packageGroups.title: Think
packageGroups.lede: Call a model, and turn a sentence into a form that is already filled in.

packageGroups.title: Reach someone
packageGroups.lede: Mail and conversation, so a product can talk to a person or an agent under the same rules.

packageGroups.title: Show the work
packageGroups.lede: Pages, lists, type, and writing that lives in the repository instead of a CMS.

packageGroups.title: Stay up
packageGroups.lede: The quiet parts that keep a public endpoint from falling over.

packageGroups.title: Get paid
packageGroups.lede: A website can take a payment. The money goes to the person being paid, not into an account the website holds.

ai-kit.what: Which model to call, whether the vendor still serves it, and what to do when every one of them fails.
ai-kit.why: Fourteen apps needed a model. The first copy picked one vendor and broke when that vendor had a bad day. The second copy would have done it again. ai-kit is the last copy: one chain, one way to tell a rate limit from an outage, one shared daily pool.
ai-kit.how: You name the job, not the vendor. The kit walks a fallback chain, classifies a 429 into the three kinds that are not the same failure, and rations a shared daily allowance so one app cannot empty the free tiers for the others. When every vendor fails, it says so instead of inventing an answer.
ai-kit.fits: The Cat, the intake forms, the research tools and the agents in Loki all think through this. A product that calls a model and does not use it is writing the second copy.

ai-forms.what: Fill a form from prose, then refine it in conversation. Headless, so every app keeps its own look.
ai-forms.why: People do not want to meet a form. They want to say what they need. Each product was about to build its own 'paste a paragraph, get fields' box, with its own prompt and its own way of being wrong.
ai-forms.how: A headless core turns prose into the fields a schema already allows, then lets the person correct them in conversation. A React hook and a route factory are optional. The form on the page stays the product's own.
ai-forms.fits: It is how a sentence becomes a listing, an application, or an intake, on top of ai-kit. The studio's bet is that the interface to an economic life is closer to speech than to a spreadsheet.

mail-kit.what: One email layer for every app. Never throws — it returns whether the mail was sent.
mail-kit.why: Email is where products quietly grow a second, private implementation: a different sender, a swallowed error, a test message that reaches a real person. Eleven apps had started.
mail-kit.how: Resend, over raw fetch, with no other dependencies. The call returns a result that says whether the mail went, rather than throwing and hoping a catch exists. Sandbox and placeholder addresses are refused, and the shared sender is one convention.
mail-kit.fits: Hire, notifications, and anything that has to reach a person outside the product. It is the boring half of 'reach someone'. threadkit is the half that stays inside.

threadkit.what: Message threads where permission is participation — not a role column. An AI obeys the same rules as a person.
threadkit.why: A chat that special-cases the assistant becomes a second permissions system. The assistant sees things the person cannot, or the person sees the assistant's notes. Both are bugs.
threadkit.how: A thread is a set of participants. Unread is per person. An AI can be a participant, and it sees exactly what its participation allows, which is the same rule as everyone else. No markup, no transport: the app keeps those.
threadkit.fits: OrangeCat, Heidi and Vita already share a conversation this way. It is how a person and an agent inhabit one room, which is the shape Loki dispatches and OrangeCat will live in.

bip-kit.what: Blog, roadmap and changelog from repo-authored markdown. Typed blocks, your design tokens on top.
bip-kit.why: Writing that lives in a CMS drifts from the product. Writing that is a pile of regexes drifts from itself. The studio writes in the repository, reviewed like code, and needed one dialect.
bip-kit.how: Markdown in, typed blocks out: headings, figures, a table of contents, reading time. A reference React renderer is optional. Bring your own tokens; the kit does not own your look. A chart fence that is malformed fails at build time rather than on the reader's screen.
bip-kit.fits: It is how the studio builds in public. OrangeCat's articles, Evig, Botsmann, DataCat and the others render through it, so a claim on a page and a claim in a commit are the same text.

sitekit.what: A website as data — a closed set of section shapes, validated, with per-field provenance.
sitekit.why: A generated site that cannot say where each sentence came from will eventually say something nobody wrote. The second generator was about to ship that.
sitekit.how: Sections are a closed union, checked before render. One set of React renderers draws them. Every field can carry where it came from, so a page can show that a line was supplied rather than invented.
sitekit.fits: Loki can stand up a site because the site is data. sitekit is that data. design-tokens is what it looks like. bip-kit is the long writing inside it.

design-tokens.what: One tokens.css behind the products, so a retheme is an edit to one file.
design-tokens.why: Color, type and radius were being copied into each app and then drifting. A retheme meant a hunt. Dark mode meant a second hunt.
design-tokens.how: Primitives, then semantic names, as CSS custom properties. Tailwind points at the variables and holds no literal color of its own. A product themes by overriding the variables, not by forking the components.
design-tokens.fits: It is why the studio can look like one studio. OrangeCat, Loki and Solon share it. A package that draws a page is expected to use these tokens rather than invent a palette.

listkit.what: A list as a query: facets, a URL you can share, sorting that puts missing values last. No markup.
listkit.why: Directories — foundations, products, people — kept reinventing filters, and each one encoded the filter in a slightly different URL, so a view could not be sent to someone else.
listkit.how: A closed set of facet kinds, a URL codec that copies the query instead of rebuilding it, a comparator that sorts missing values last, and page math that cannot produce a negative offset. No React and no HTTP client.
listkit.fits: Hirnli's foundation lists and Loki's project lists are the same idea. A list you can link is part of how the studio's work stays checkable.

limitkit.what: Rate limiting as a decision, not middleware. Bounded memory by construction, standard headers.
limitkit.why: Public routes were growing one-off counters that forgot to bound themselves, and that told the client nothing when they said no. The failure mode is a process that remembers every IP forever.
limitkit.how: Fixed and sliding windows over a store you pass in, with a bounded in-memory store as the default. The decision is separate from the framework. The response carries the standard rate-limit headers, and the client IP is read in one place.
limitkit.fits: It is what lets a small studio leave a door open — hire, pay links, public APIs — without one caller becoming the outage. Eight apps already depend on that being true.

paykit.what: Classify pasted Bitcoin receive strings and describe payment rails a site can show. It does not hold keys or verify settlement.
paykit.why: A site may need to tell a payer where to send money without becoming a wallet or custodian. paykit provides small, framework-free helpers for that boundary.
paykit.how: classifyPaste() recognizes supported Bitcoin URI, Lightning-address, and Nostr Wallet Connect forms; shownRail() describes a display-only rail and its supplied payload. The host app still renders the payment instructions, validates destinations before saving, and verifies payment itself. paykit does not check address checksums, create invoices, process payments, or confirm settlement.
paykit.fits: Use it when an app needs to classify a pasted receive destination or represent a payment code supplied by the app. It is a published utility package, not a payment processor; the current fleet registry finds no app manifest adopting it yet.
